translation_en: Yahya ibn Bukayr narrated to us: Al-Layth narrated to us, from ‘Uqayl. Ibn Shihab said: ‘Urwah ibn al-Zubayr informed me that ‘Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: I have never known my parents except that they followed the religion. Not a day passed without the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, coming to us at both ends of the day, in the morning and the evening. When the Muslims were put to trial, Abu Bakr set out as an emigrant toward the land of Abyssinia. When he reached Bark al-Ghimad, Ibn al-Dughunnah met him. He was the chief of the Qarah. He said, ‘Where are you going, Abu Bakr?’ Abu Bakr said, ‘My people have driven me out, so I want to travel through the land and worship my Lord.’ Ibn al-Dughunnah said, ‘Someone like you, Abu Bakr, should neither leave nor be driven out. You help the destitute, maintain family ties, bear the burden of the helpless, host guests, and assist people when they face rightful hardships. I will protect you. Return and worship your Lord in your own land.’ Abu Bakr returned, and Ibn al-Dughunnah travelled with him. That evening Ibn al-Dughunnah went around to the leading men of Quraysh and said to them, ‘Someone like Abu Bakr should neither leave nor be driven out. Would you drive out a man who helps the destitute, maintains family ties, bears the burden of the helpless, hosts guests, and assists people when they face rightful hardships?’ Quraysh did not reject Ibn al-Dughunnah’s protection. They said to him, ‘Tell Abu Bakr to worship his Lord in his home. Let him pray there and recite whatever he wishes, but let him not trouble us by doing that, and let him not do it openly. We fear that he will tempt our women and children.’ Ibn al-Dughunnah told Abu Bakr this. Abu Bakr stayed that way, worshipping his Lord in his home. He did not pray openly or recite outside his home. Then Abu Bakr decided to build a mosque in the courtyard of his home. He prayed and recited the Quran there. The women and children of the polytheists began gathering around him, amazed at him and watching him. Abu Bakr was a man who wept readily; he could not hold back his tears when he recited the Quran. This alarmed the leading polytheists of Quraysh, so they sent for Ibn al-Dughunnah, who came to them. They said, ‘We gave Abu Bakr protection through you on the condition that he worship his Lord in his home. He has gone beyond that and built a mosque in the courtyard of his home, where he prays and recites aloud. We fear that he will tempt our women and children, so stop him. If he wishes to limit himself to worshipping his Lord in his home, he may do so. But if he insists on doing it openly, ask him to return your pledge of protection to you. We dislike betraying you, but we do not accept Abu Bakr’s public worship.’ ‘Aishah said: Ibn al-Dughunnah went to Abu Bakr and said, ‘You know the terms on which I made an agreement with you. Either you limit yourself to that, or you return my protection to me. I do not want the Arabs to hear that I failed to protect a man to whom I had given my pledge.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘I return your protection to you, and I am content with the protection of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.’ At that time the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, was in Makkah. He said to the Muslims, ‘I have been shown the place of your emigration: a land of palm trees between two lava fields.’ These are the two rocky lava fields. Some people emigrated toward Madinah, and most of those who had emigrated to Abyssinia returned to Madinah. Abu Bakr prepared to travel toward Madinah. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said to him, ‘Wait. I hope that I will be given permission.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘May my father be sacrificed for you. Do you hope for that?’ He said, ‘Yes.’ Abu Bakr kept himself ready to accompany the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. For four months he fed the two riding camels he had with leaves of the acacia tree, which is called khabat. Ibn Shihab said: ‘Urwah said: ‘Aishah said: One day, while we were sitting in Abu Bakr’s house in the heat of midday, someone said to Abu Bakr, ‘Here is the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, with his face covered. He has come at an hour when he does not usually visit us.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘May my father and mother be sacrificed for him. By Allah, something must have brought him at this hour.’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, came, asked permission to enter, and was admitted. The Prophet said to Abu Bakr, ‘Send away those who are with you.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘They are your family, may my father be sacrificed for you, Messenger of Allah.’ He said, ‘I have been given permission to set out.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘May my father be sacrificed for you, Messenger of Allah, may I accompany you?’ The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said, ‘Yes.’ Abu Bakr said, ‘Take one of these two riding camels, may my father be sacrificed for you, Messenger of Allah.’ The Messenger of Allah said, ‘At its price.’ ‘Aishah said: We prepared both of them as quickly as we could and made food for them in a leather bag. Asma’ bint Abi Bakr cut a piece from her waistband and tied the opening of the bag with it. For that reason she was called the woman with the waistband. Then the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and Abu Bakr reached a cave on Mount Thawr and hid there for three nights. ‘Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, a sharp and perceptive young man, spent the nights with them. At dawn he slipped away from them and spent the day among Quraysh in Makkah, as though he had slept there. He heard any plan being made against them and retained it, then brought them news of it when darkness deepened. ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah, Abu Bakr’s freedman, grazed a flock of milch sheep for them. After part of the night had passed, he brought the flock to them. They spent the night with its milk and heated milk. At daybreak, ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah drove the flock away. He did this on each of those three nights. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, and Abu Bakr hired a man from Banu al-Dayl, from Banu ‘Abd ibn ‘Adi, as a highly skilled guide. He had an alliance with the family of al-‘As ibn Wa’il al-Sahmi, while following the religion of the unbelievers of Quraysh, but they trusted him. They gave him their two riding camels and arranged to meet him at the cave of Thawr after three nights, with their camels, on the morning of the third day. ‘Amir ibn Fuhayrah and the guide set out with them, and the guide took them along the coastal route.’
